weeks.title: ML Evaluation & Experiment Tracking
weeks.mindset: Coming from the ML specialization: you know how to train a model — now learn how to prove one works. Modern AI engineering is measurement-first: every model claim needs a number, a baseline, and a dataset behind it.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can set up an MLflow experiment, log train/CV/test metrics for two competing models, and write a one-paragraph verdict on which to ship and why.

tasks.content: Study train/validation/test methodology properly — read about data leakage and write down 3 ways it can sneak into a pipeline.
Learn what an experiment tracker does: runs, params, metrics, artifacts. Skim the MLflow quickstart.
Learn error analysis: slice your validation set, find the worst-performing segments, and read about evaluation datasets (fixed benchmark sets vs random splits).
Read an introduction to A/B testing concepts — hypothesis, control, significance, and why offline metrics don't always predict online wins.
Install MLflow locally. Re-run your ML Week 3 logistic regression and ML Week 5 digit recognizer as tracked experiments with logged params and metrics.
Log a confusion matrix and per-class metrics as artifacts. Compare the two runs in the MLflow UI.
Learn LLM evaluation concepts: retrieval evaluation, hallucination measurement, response-quality scoring. Skim LangSmith's evaluation docs.
Cross-link: revisit GenAI Roadmap Week 13 — RAG Evaluation & Safety Guardrails for the RAGAS-style evaluation mindset you'll build on here.
Mini-project: build an evaluation pipeline that loads a dataset, scores two models (one baseline, one contender), logs everything to MLflow, and prints a comparison report.
Explain out loud, without notes: overfitting to the validation set, why leakage is fatal, and what an A/B test adds that an offline eval can't.

weeks.title: SQL & Data Engineering Fundamentals
weeks.mindset: Coming from notebooks: data doesn't arrive as a clean CSV. Real systems pull from databases and APIs, and the engineer who can write the SQL and build the pipeline controls the quality of everything downstream.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can write joins and window-function queries in PostgreSQL, load data with DuckDB, and run a reproducible ETL script that validates its own output.

tasks.content: Learn/review SQL fundamentals: SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, JOINs. If you know these cold, go straight to window functions.
Learn window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG/LEAD) — the single biggest SQL power-up for analytics work.
Learn the shape of an ETL pipeline: extract → validate → transform → load. Learn what data validation means (schema, nulls, ranges, uniqueness).
Understand batch vs streaming at a concept level, and when an API is the right data source.
Set up PostgreSQL locally (Docker is fine). Load a dataset and write 10 queries: joins, aggregates, and 3 window-function queries.
Try DuckDB on the same dataset — query a Parquet file directly and note when you'd reach for it instead of Postgres.
Learn Pandas vs Polars: when DataFrame ergonomics matter and what lazy evaluation buys you on larger data.
Skim Airflow basics — DAGs, tasks, schedules. You don't need to master it; know what problem it solves.
Mini-project: build an ETL script that pulls from a public API, validates the rows (schema + sanity checks), transforms them, and loads into Postgres. It should fail loudly on bad data.
Explain without notes: why validate at ingestion (not at model-training time), and what batch vs streaming means for your pipeline design.

weeks.title: MLOps I — Serving with FastAPI + Docker
weeks.mindset: The wall every learner hits: a model in a notebook is a science project; a model behind an API is a product. This week you cross that wall permanently.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday your digit-recognizer (or another ML model) is served by a FastAPI app inside a Docker container, with health checks and a /predict endpoint that returns typed responses.

tasks.content: Learn model serving patterns: batch scoring vs online inference, request/response schemas, latency budgets.
Learn the anatomy of a Docker image for an ML service: base image, dependencies, model artifacts, CMD.
Study model versioning: why you pin model versions alongside code, and how artifacts flow from training to serving.
Cross-link: you already know FastAPI from GenAI Roadmap Week 2 — Async + FastAPI. Skim your notes; this week you point it at an ML model instead of an LLM.
Wrap your trained model in a FastAPI app: /predict endpoint, Pydantic request/response models, input validation.
Add a /health endpoint and write a smoke test that posts a sample and asserts the response shape.
Write the Dockerfile, build the image, and run the container locally. Keep the image lean (multi-stage build if you can).
Cross-link: GenAI Roadmap Week 22 — Docker Containers & AWS ECS Cloud Deploy covers Docker + cloud deploy in depth; you'll go further there.
Mini-project: dockerize the full service (app + model), push to a registry, and document the run command in the README. Someone else should be able to run it with one command.
Explain without notes: what breaks when a model is served (drift, latency, cold starts) and how versioning + health checks catch it early.

weeks.title: MLOps II — Monitoring, Logging & Rollbacks
weeks.mindset: Deployment is day one, not the finish line. Real systems degrade quietly. This week you learn the instrumentation that tells you a model is sick before your users do.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday your served model emits structured logs and metrics, you can simulate a bad deployment, and you can roll back to the previous model version cleanly.

tasks.content: Learn what to monitor in production ML: latency, throughput, error rate, prediction distribution drift, and input-data sanity.
Learn structured logging basics — JSON logs, correlation ids, and why grep-ability saves you at 3am.
Learn rollback strategies: blue/green, shadow deploys, keeping N-1 model artifacts warm.
Learn cost & latency optimization concepts: batching, caching, smaller artifacts, right-sizing containers.
Add structured JSON logging and request-duration metrics to your FastAPI model service from Week 3.
Ship those logs to stdout and view them with docker logs; write a tiny script that tails the log and computes p50/p95 latency.
Implement model versioning at serve time: the service loads model version from an env var, and two versions can coexist as two containers on different ports.
Cross-link: GenAI Roadmap Week 24 — LLMOps & Portfolio Polish is the LLM-flavoured version of this week; do that week's monitoring tasks for parity.
Mini-project: simulate a bad deploy (swap in a corrupted model), detect it via your health check + metrics, roll back to N-1, and write a short postmortem (what fired, what lagged).
Explain without notes: the four signals of model degradation and which one users notice first.

title: Phase 2 — Transformer & LLM Internals
hours: ~20 hours · know what's inside the box

weeks.title: Transformers — Attention & Architecture
weeks.mindset: You've used LLMs as APIs. Now open the box: tokenization, embeddings, attention, transformer blocks. The goal is understanding and adapting — not training GPT from scratch.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can walk through a transformer forward pass on a whiteboard: token → embedding → attention → block → logits, and explain why attention needs Q/K/V.

tasks.content: Learn tokenization: BPE, WordPiece, why vocab size matters, and why "strawberry has 3 r's" broke models.
Learn embeddings as lookup tables — and connect them to the embedding models you used in GenAI Roadmap Week 9.
Learn attention from the ground up: queries, keys, values, scaled dot-product, softmax over similarities. Watch 3Blue1Brown's attention video twice if needed.
Learn self-attention vs cross-attention, and multi-head attention (why multiple heads, what each head can specialize to).
Implement scaled dot-product attention in raw NumPy (you did forward prop this way in ML Week 5 — same spirit). Verify shapes and softmax rows sum to 1.
Implement positional encoding (sinusoidal) and add it to your toy embeddings. Note what breaks without it.
Learn the full transformer block: residual connections, layer norm, feed-forward, stacking. Sketch the data shapes through one block.
Learn pretraining vs instruction tuning at a concept level: next-token prediction, SFT, RLHF/DPO in one sentence each.
Mini-project: assemble a one-block toy transformer in PyTorch (attention + FFN + residuals) and run a forward pass on a 4-token sentence. Print every intermediate shape.
Cross-link: GenAI Roadmap Week 25 — Transformer Internals & LLM Fine-Tuning is the deep-dive version of this week; use it as your reference track.
Whiteboard the full forward pass without notes: "the cat sat" → tokens → logits. Explain why attention is O(n²) and why context windows are expensive.

weeks.title: Fine-Tuning, LoRA & Adaptation
weeks.focus_hours: 10 hours · adapting models, not training them
weeks.mindset: Engineer's rule: prompt → RAG → fine-tune, in that order of cost. This week you learn what fine-tuning actually changes and when it earns its cost.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can explain what LoRA freezes and what it trains, run a small fine-tune on a toy task, and justify in writing when NOT to fine-tune.

tasks.content: Learn the adaptation ladder: prompting → few-shot → RAG → fine-tuning → pretraining. Write the cost/benefit of each rung in one line.
Learn what SFT (supervised fine-tuning) does to a base model — format, tone, task specialization — vs what RAG does (knowledge injection).
Learn LoRA / PEFT: low-rank adapter matrices, frozen base weights, why memory drops dramatically. Understand rank (r) and alpha intuitively.
Learn quantization basics (what QLoRA builds on): INT8/4-bit, what precision loss means for quality.
Prepare a fine-tuning dataset: 100+ instruction/response pairs for a small, well-defined task (e.g. extract structured fields from messy text).
Set up PyTorch properly (GPU or Colab). Sanity-check you can load a small open model and run inference.
Run a LoRA fine-tune of a small model on your dataset (HuggingFace PEFT is fine). Watch the loss curve; note training time and memory.
Evaluate before/after on a held-out set of your task. If quality didn't move, diagnose: dataset size? task ambiguity? wrong rung of the ladder?
Mini-project: wrap your fine-tuned adapter in an eval: 20 held-out examples, before/after scores, and a written verdict — ship, or drop back to prompting/RAG.
Explain without notes: what LoRA freezes, what it trains, and the three questions you ask before choosing fine-tuning over RAG.

title: Phase 3 — LLM Systems at Production Grade

weeks.title: Production RAG — Retrieval Engineering
weeks.mindset: You built RAG in the GenAI roadmap. This week is the hardening pass: chunking strategy, hybrid search, re-ranking, and retrieval evaluation as a first-class metric.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can take a naive RAG pipeline and improve its retrieval metrics measurably — and prove the improvement with a scored eval set.

tasks.content: Study chunking strategies: fixed, recursive, semantic, parent-child. Write when each wins.
Cross-link: revisit GenAI Roadmap Week 12 — Context Enrichment & Parent-Child Retrieval — you implemented the pattern; now study why it works.
Learn hybrid search: BM25 + dense vectors, reciprocal rank fusion. Know when lexical beats semantic and vice versa.
Learn re-ranking: cross-encoders vs bi-encoders, and the recall-then-rerank pattern.
Build a hybrid retrieval pipeline (BM25 + embeddings + fusion) over a document set. Compare top-k quality vs pure vector search by eye.
Add a cross-encoder re-ranker stage and measure latency impact alongside quality.
Build a retrieval eval set: 30 queries with known-relevant chunks. Score precision@k and recall@k for your pipeline variants.
Cross-link: GenAI Roadmap Week 11 — Production Retrieval (Hybrid Search & Re-ranking) is the sibling week; cross-check your implementation against it.
Mini-project: baseline vs improved RAG — one command, one table of metrics (retrieval + end-to-end answer quality), one written recommendation.
Explain without notes: why hybrid beats pure vector on keyword-heavy queries, and where a re-ranker pays for its latency.

weeks.title: Agents & Tool Use — Hardened Patterns
weeks.mindset: Agents fail in production for boring reasons: unclear stopping conditions, unbounded tool loops, no human gate on risky actions. This week is about the guardrails that make agents shippable.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can take an agent workflow and add: a tool budget, a human-approval gate, structured state, and a trace you can debug after the fact.

tasks.content: Study agent architecture: the loop (observe → think → act), stopping conditions, and failure modes when the loop never terminates.
Learn planning patterns: plan-then-execute vs ReAct-style interleaving, and when each degrades.
Learn memory systems: short-term (context window), episodic (past runs), semantic (knowledge store). Know what belongs in each.
Learn agent security: prompt injection through tool output, least-privilege tools, allow-lists. One real attack writeup read end-to-end.
Take an existing agent (yours from GenAI Week 14, or a fresh LangGraph one) and add a tool-call budget + step ceiling that hard-stops runaway loops.
Add structured tracing: every step logged (thought, tool, args, result) to a store you can query after a run.
Add a human-in-the-loop gate: risky tool calls (delete, spend, send) pause for approval. You built this pattern in GenAI Week 8 — port it.
Cross-link: GenAI Roadmap Weeks 14–17 (agent architectures → production agent workflows) are your reference tracks; skim Week 17 for production checklists.
Mini-project: an agent that completes a real multi-tool workflow (research → draft → approve → execute) with budget, HITL gate, and a full trace for the audit.
Explain without notes: the three guardrails every production agent needs, and the failure each one prevents.

weeks.title: Multi-Agent Systems & MCP
weeks.mindset: Multi-agent is not more agents — it's better boundaries. Supervisor patterns, specialized roles, and MCP as the standard socket between agents and tools.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you can explain when a multi-agent split pays off, run a supervisor + workers pattern, and expose a tool over MCP that any client can consume.

tasks.content: Study multi-agent patterns: supervisor, hierarchical, sequential pipelines. Write down when one good agent beats a committee.
Learn role specialization: researcher/writer/critic splits and how context is passed between agents without bloat.
Learn MCP (Model Context Protocol) anatomy: servers, tools, resources, transports. You built MCP servers in GenAI Week 18 — refresh the architecture.
Cross-link: GenAI Roadmap Week 18 — MCP Architecture and Week 19 — Database-backed MCP Servers; this week you treat MCP as shared infrastructure for multi-agent setups.
Build a supervisor + 2 workers system (LangGraph or CrewAI): supervisor routes, workers execute, state flows through a typed graph.
Expose one worker's tool as an MCP server and have the other worker call it through the protocol.
Add an evaluation harness for the multi-agent run: task success, cost per run, tokens per agent. Compare against a single-agent baseline.
Stress it: give an ambiguous task and watch routing. Log where it dithers.
Mini-project: a documented multi-agent workflow with MCP tooling, a cost dashboard, and a written verdict: multi-agent vs single-agent for this task class.
Explain without notes: the supervisor pattern's failure mode, and what MCP standardizes that raw function-calling doesn't.

weeks.title: LLM Evaluation & Observability
weeks.mindset: LLM systems fail probabilistically — the same input can be right today and wrong tomorrow. Evaluation isn't a phase; it's the instrument panel you keep running forever.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday you have an eval suite for an LLM app (retrieval + answer quality + hallucination rate) that runs in CI and blocks regressions.

tasks.content: Study LLM-as-judge patterns: rubric scoring, pairwise comparison, known biases (position, verbosity, self-preference).
Learn hallucination measurement: faithfulness-to-context metrics, groundedness checks, citation verification.
Learn observability for LLM apps: traces (LangSmith/OpenTelemetry), cost tracking, latency breakdown by stage.
Cross-link: GenAI Roadmap Week 13 — RAG Evaluation & Safety Guardrails covered RAGAS; now add end-to-end answer evals on top.
Build an eval dataset for your RAG app from Week 7: 50 questions, reference answers, expected sources.
Implement three scorers: retrieval recall, answer faithfulness (LLM-judge), answer correctness (LLM-judge with rubric). Log per-question results.
Wire the eval suite into CI (GitHub Actions): run on PR, fail the build if scores drop beyond a threshold.
Add trace sampling: a slice of production-style traffic traced end-to-end, reviewed weekly.
Mini-project: a regression dashboard — eval scores over time, per-category breakdown, and an alert when any metric crosses its threshold.
Explain without notes: the three biases of LLM-judges and the one mitigation for each.

weeks.title: Capstone I — Build the System
weeks.mindset: Portfolio rule: one system that demonstrates evaluation + deployment + judgment beats ten tutorial apps. Pick something real, measure it, ship it.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday your capstone skeleton runs end-to-end locally: data pipeline → model/LLM core → API → eval harness, all in version control with CI.

tasks.content: Pick the capstone: a production-grade RAG assistant, an evaluated multi-agent workflow, or a fine-tuned-model product. One page: users, inputs, outputs, success metrics.
Write the eval plan before the code: datasets, metrics, thresholds. If you can't define success, the project isn't scoped yet.
Build the data layer: ingestion pipeline (from Week 2 patterns) feeding the app. Validate at ingestion.
Build the core: model or LLM pipeline behind a clean interface, with the adapter/versioning pattern from Week 3.
Build the API surface (FastAPI), structured logging, health checks — the Week 3–4 serving stack, reused.
Containerize it. One command runs the whole system (docker compose is fine).
Wire in the eval harness (Week 10): eval dataset, scorers, CI gate on PRs.
Log everything to your tracker from Week 1 — this project is an MLflow/LangSmith experiment too.
End-to-end smoke run: fresh clone → one command → working system → passing evals. Fix the friction a stranger would hit.
Write the README: architecture diagram, eval results table, run instructions. This is the artifact recruiters and reviewers see first.

weeks.title: Capstone II — Deploy, Monitor, Defend
weeks.mindset: Shipped beats perfect. Deploy it on real infrastructure, watch it under real traffic (even 10 requests), and write the honest engineering story of what you measured and what you'd change.
weeks.weekly_goal: By Sunday the capstone is live on a public URL, monitored, with an eval-report page — and you can defend every design decision in a 10-minute walkthrough.

tasks.content: Deploy to real infrastructure — cloud (AWS/GCP/Fly/Render). Not localhost. You did ECS in GenAI Week 22; reuse that playbook.
Wire in monitoring: uptime check, latency metrics, error alerts, cost tracking.
Publish an eval report page: current scores, trend, per-category breakdown. Make quality visible, not claimed.
Run a load sanity test: 100 requests, p95 latency, cost per 1000 requests. Note the ceiling.
Perform one incident drill: break something on purpose, verify the alert fires, roll back, write the two-paragraph postmortem.
Harden: rate limiting, input validation, secrets handling. Second pass on the security checklist from Week 8.
Polish the README + add the project to your portfolio site with a link to the live system and the eval report.
Record/draft the 10-minute walkthrough: problem → architecture → evals → results → trade-offs. This is your interview story.
Full review of the Post-ML track: reread all 12 weekly goals, verify each mini-project is in version control with its eval evidence, and mark the gaps honestly.
Write the final reflection in the journal: what you can now build that you couldn't before the ML specialization, and the next 90 days of deliberate practice.
